title: Spiritual Habits: A Bible Study on Formation
subtitle: A five-session study on habits, desire, and the slow work of being formed.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has known the right thing and couldn't do it, who has filled the head with correct belief and watched the life go on unchanged, and for small groups tired of a discipleship that hands more information to people who already have plenty. Its five sessions take up an old truth the church nearly forgot: we're shaped less by what we think than by what we love, and love is trained by what we repeat. It looks plainly at the habits already forming us, the phone and the feed and the store, and asks what they're aiming the heart at. It recovers the historic spiritual disciplines as counter-formation. It refuses the false war between grace and effort. And it ends with a rule of life small enough that an ordinary person could keep it. It's built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries notes on what it's after, and every session ends in prayer.

Most of us live in the gap between the theology we could pass a test on and the people we actually are. I do. We assumed we'd be made holy by getting our thinking straight, and we weren't. So the one thing this study won't do is turn formation into a performance you put on to earn God's favor. The disciplines aren't the price of grace. They're how grace, already given, gets down into the muscles. We don't train to be loved. We train because we already are.
audience: Individuals, small groups, and anyone tired of a faith that stays in the head

sessions.title: You Are Not What You Think, You Are What You Love
sessions.aim: To see that a person is shaped less by what she believes than by what she loves, and that love isn't settled in a single moment but trained by repetition. The session refuses two mistakes: the idea that right ideas are enough, and the idea that we should wait for the right feelings to arrive on their own.
sessions.summary:
Many Christians assume they'll be made holy by thinking, that if they stack up enough correct belief they'll come out changed. They can pass any doctrine test you hand them. They still lose their temper with the people they love, still keep the habits they despise, still can't become by thinking the people they can so clearly describe. That gap is the subject of this whole study.

The philosopher James K.A. Smith opens You Are What You Love with a question that takes the floor out from under us: what if we're shaped more by what we love than by what we know? Augustine saw it sixteen centuries ago. He began the Confessions by telling God that our hearts are restless until they rest in him, and in the City of God he called virtue rightly ordered love.

The case for putting belief first deserves a full hearing. Truth matters, feelings are unreliable, and a faith built on emotion collapses. All of that is true. But belief alone can't explain the oldest fact of the Christian life, that we know the good and don't do it. We're changed by what we practice until it becomes what we want. You are what you love, and what you love was trained into you by what you've repeated.

keyScripture.why: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life" (Proverbs 4:23). The heart, the place of love and desire, is the spring the whole life runs from, so guarding and aiming it matters more than stocking the head.

discussion.q: Where have you believed that more information would finally change you? What has that assumption cost you?
discussion.behind: Start with the default nearly everyone in the room is running: the quiet belief that the problem is a knowledge problem, and one more book or sermon will close the gap. Bring the assumption into the open before you offer anything else. The point isn't to look down on learning. It's to notice the distance between what people know and who they've become.

discussion.q: Think of a habit you can't seem to break by deciding to. What might it show about what you actually love, underneath what you say you believe?
discussion.behind: Move from the idea to the person's own life. A habit that survives every good intention is usually pointing at a real love: comfort, control, escape, being liked. The head has never managed to argue it down. Help the room treat the stubborn habit as information about the heart, not only as a failure of willpower.

discussion.q: Some Christians answer this session by saying truth has to come first, because a faith built on feeling falls apart. What's right about that? Where does putting belief first still leave a person stuck?
discussion.behind: Give the belief-first view its full due. Truth isn't optional, and emotion is a poor foundation. Then name the limit: correct belief has never on its own produced a changed life, which is why the New Testament talks so much about training and practice and not only about believing the right things.

discussion.q: Augustine said virtue is rightly ordered love, that the question isn't whether you love but what you love most, and in what order. If someone watched an ordinary week of your life, what would they say you love most?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. The trouble is rarely too much love. It's love aimed at the wrong things, or the right things in the wrong order. Let people read their calendar and their attention as a picture of what they actually worship. Keep it gentle, and don't let it turn into a show or into despair.

discussion.q: Children learn what to love by watching what the adults around them repeat, more than by hearing what those adults believe. Who's learning their loves from your habits, and what might you be teaching them without meaning to?
discussion.behind: Widen the question to the people around us. We're always passing on loves through practice, to children, spouses and friends, whether we mean to or not. Go first if the room is slow. You're after recognition, not guilt.

objections.objection: This makes doctrine optional and turns Christianity into feelings. If you stop putting truth first, you end up with a soft faith that believes whatever feels good.
objections.response: The fear is guarding something real, so grant it. Truth isn't optional, feelings are unreliable, and a faith that floats free of doctrine will drift toward whatever the culture is selling. But saying a person is shaped by love doesn't mean belief doesn't matter. It means belief alone has never been enough, and that's just a plain report of the Christian life. Paul doesn't tell the Romans to think harder. He tells them to "present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Romans 12:1) and to "be transformed by the renewal of your mind" (Romans 12:2), and that renewal comes through a whole life offered, not only through information. Right belief is necessary. It isn't sufficient. The head can be orthodox while the heart is aimed somewhere else entirely.

objections.objection: I know people who go through all the religious motions and aren't changed at all. Habits and practices are empty ritual. What matters is a real relationship with God.
objections.response: Dead ritual is real, and the prophets hated it as much as you do. God said of his people that they "draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me" (Isaiah 29:13), and Jesus quoted those words against the religious leaders of his day. But there's a false choice inside the objection, between empty ritual and a relationship with no practices at all. The second thing doesn't exist. Every relationship is carried by habits, the daily ways we turn toward the other person, and a relationship with God that has no practices isn't more real. Usually it's just fading. The trouble with dead ritual isn't that it's a practice. It's a practice cut off from love. The answer is to let the practices become again what they were meant to be, a frame a real love can grow along.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the one thing you believe with your whole head and contradict with your whole week, and what does that tell you about what you actually love?
sessions.practice: This week, for three ordinary days, keep a plain record of where your attention and your minutes actually go, not where you wish they went. Don't fix anything yet. Just look. At the end, ask what a stranger reading only that record would say you love most, and write down the gap between that answer and the one you'd give out loud.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us to love you, and we've loaded our hearts onto a hundred smaller things and called it living. We've believed the right things about you with heads that pass every test, and walked out into weeks that serve a different god. Forgive the gap. Search us, and show us what we actually love, in the order we actually love it, and reorder us gently toward yourself. Teach us that you're not asking first for better arguments but for our hearts, and that even our loving is something you give before you ask for it. Keep our hearts, since the whole of life flows from them. Amen.
reflection: Where have I assumed that knowing more would finally change me, and how long have I been waiting for information to do what only love and practice can do?
What does a plain look at my week show that I love most, and is it what I'd say I love if someone asked me?
If my loves were trained into me by repetition, what have I been repeating, and what has it been teaching my heart to want?
sessions.teaching:
Most of us carry a picture of the Christian life that we've never examined. We assume that becoming a Christian is mostly a matter of getting our thinking straight, and that we'll grow holy by gathering correct beliefs and stacking them high enough to stand on. Plenty of us could pass any doctrine test put in front of us. And we still lose our temper with the people we love most, still keep the habits we privately despise, still can't become, by thinking, the people we can describe so well. That gap is where this study lives. It's the oldest open secret of the Christian life: the head can be fully persuaded while the life goes on as before.

James K.A. Smith opens his book You Are What You Love with a question that gets underneath that picture. What if we're shaped more by what we love than by what we know? What if a human being is, at bottom, less a thinking thing than a wanting one? Smith argues that we absorbed the other picture without noticing. He describes it as treating people like brains on a stick, minds that happen to be carried around by bodies, containers that become holy once you pour in enough right information. And we built a lot of church life to match. If people are just under-informed, then more sermons and more studies and more content should fix them. It hasn't, and Smith says it was never going to, because that isn't the kind of creature a human being is.

Augustine saw this long before. He began the Confessions by telling God that our hearts are restless until they rest in him, which puts the engine of a life not in the intellect but in a heart that's always leaning toward something it hopes will satisfy it. Later, in the City of God, he described virtue as the right ordering of love. That means the problem in us is rarely that we love too much. It's that we love the wrong things, or love good things in the wrong order. Scripture had said it first: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life" (Proverbs 4:23). And Jesus put it in a sentence we usually read backward: "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). The heart follows the treasure. Where we put our attention and our time is where our love goes.

I want to give the other side its full hearing, because thoughtful believers make it and it guards something precious. Truth matters, they say, and they're right. Feelings are unreliable, and they're right about that too. A faith built on emotion rather than on what's true will collapse the first time the emotion runs out. I'd never want this study to suggest that doctrine is optional. That would be leading people off a cliff.

But the belief-first picture can't explain what it's actually like to follow Jesus. It can't explain why a person can affirm every line of the creed and still be anxious, harsh and greedy on an ordinary Tuesday, bound to the very things he can explain are hurting him. If information were enough, the best-informed Christians would be the most changed, and anyone who has spent time in a church knows that isn't so. I know it isn't so in me. My problem was never mainly that I didn't know enough. My loves had been trained, for years, by a thousand repetitions I never examined, and believing the right things didn't retrain them on its own.

That's what we tend to miss. Love isn't a decision you make once, and it isn't a feeling that drops on you from the sky. It's more like a habit, formed the way every habit is formed, by repetition, until the thing you've practiced becomes the thing you want without trying. Aristotle saw part of this long before Christ: in the Nicomachean Ethics he argued that we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones. Character isn't chosen fresh each morning. It's worn into us. The church knew this for most of its history, which is why it gave people prayers to repeat and a Table to come back to, and then a lot of us forgot it in an age drowning in information.

It matters for more than ourselves. The people who live with us, and especially children, aren't learning their loves from our theology. They're learning them from what they watch us reach for when we're tired, from the reflexes we've practiced so long we no longer notice them. So the first word of this study isn't "try harder to believe." It's this: look plainly at what you love, then look at what you've been repeating, because the second shaped the first. And the God who wants your heart is patient enough to retrain it.

scriptureStudy.note: "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life." The heart, not the head alone, is named as the source the whole life flows from, which is why formation aims at desire and not only at belief.

"For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." The order is the reverse of what we assume. The heart follows the treasure, so where we invest our time and attention is where our love goes.

"You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might." The great command isn't first to think correctly about God but to love him with everything, which makes the aiming of love the whole task.
"For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks." What comes out of us under pressure isn't what we've decided to believe but what the heart is actually full of.
"Be transformed by the renewal of your mind." The renewal is real, and Paul calls it transformation, a reworking of the whole person that reaches past belief into what we want and choose.

"Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely ... think about these things." Paul asks for a repeated practice of attention, because the mind is shaped by what it dwells on again and again.

"Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart." Delight comes first, and it reshapes the desires themselves. God gives new wants to the heart that learns to delight in him.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, trace how the church lost a picture of the person it once held. James K.A. Smith, in You Are What You Love and more fully in Desiring the Kingdom, argues that the modern West took on a largely Cartesian view of the self, the person as essentially a thinking thing, and that much of the church absorbed it without noticing and rebuilt discipleship as the transfer of information. Weigh that claim. Then set it beside the older line that runs from Aristotle through Augustine to Thomas Aquinas, in which a human being is first a lover, drawn by desire toward some picture of the good life, and virtue is the long training of that desire.

Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics argues that we become just by doing just acts and temperate by doing temperate ones. Augustine made the object of love the whole question, opening the Confessions with the restless heart and, in the City of God, describing virtue as the order of love. Charles Taylor's account of the modern social imaginary adds something useful: our sense of the good life is carried less by stated beliefs than by unspoken pictures we absorb from the practices around us. C.S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity (book 3, chapter 4), makes a related point, that every choice turns the central part of us into something a little different from what it was, slowly, toward heaven or toward hell. None of this despises the mind, which is a gift. It recovers a fuller picture, in which a person is aimed by love before she's convinced by argument, and that's why growing in Christ has always needed practice and not only persuasion.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose the most theologically sharp person in your group is frustrated by this session. He's quick with a citation and can correct a bad argument before it's finished. He says the answer to a weak Christian life is better doctrine, that people fall away because they were never properly taught, and that all this talk of love and habit is a retreat from truth into feelings.

Honor his gift before you press him. He isn't wrong that truth matters, and his hunger for it is something the room needs, so say that and mean it. But notice what his frustration might be pointing at. Someone who reaches this quickly for doctrine as the cure for everything can sometimes be using the head to avoid the heart, staying inside what he's good at because the question this session asks, what do you actually love, is harder and more exposing.

Don't let the conversation shrink to whether truth counts. It does. Then ask him gently whether there's any gap in his own life between what he can defend and who he is when no one is arguing, and what that gap might be telling him. Ask the group the same question.

sessions.title: The Liturgies You Did Not Choose
sessions.aim: To see that we're already being shaped all day by practices we never chose as formation, the phone, the feed and the store, and to name what each is aiming the heart at. The session refuses both the panic that treats a device as the devil and the denial that pretends our habits are neutral.
sessions.summary:
Many of us pick up the phone the moment we wake, before we pray and before we speak to anyone we love, and we never decided to. That's the point. A liturgy, in the old sense, is a repeated bodily practice that trains a person to want something. James K.A. Smith argues that much of the formation in our lives isn't happening at church for an hour on Sunday but at the mall and on the screen every day, in practices designed to aim our love at a particular picture of the good life.

So the question isn't whether we're being formed but by what. Scripture says it bluntly: "Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them" (Psalm 115:8). We take on the character of whatever we give ourselves to.

The case that a phone is just a tool, like a hammer, has some truth in it. But a hammer doesn't reach into your pocket a hundred times a day, learn your desires and feed them back to you. The deeper cost isn't mainly the time we lose. It's the loves we gain: a heart slowly trained to want distraction over presence and the edited life over the given one. We didn't choose these liturgies. We're becoming what they repeat in us all the same.

keyScripture.why: "Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them" (Psalm 115:8). The oldest law of formation: we take on the character of whatever we worship, so the practices we give ourselves to are shaping us, whether we notice or not.

discussion.q: What's the first thing you reach for in the morning? What has that reflex been training you to want?
discussion.behind: Start with the reflex nobody chose, because everyone has one and few have looked at it. The first reach of the morning is a practice so worn in that it runs without a decision. Help people notice it without shame and begin to ask what it aims the heart at before the day has begun.

discussion.q: Smith argues that the mall and the screen shape us more than an hour at church, because they have us every day. Where is the most formative hour of your ordinary day spent, and who designed it?
discussion.behind: Do the arithmetic of attention. An hour of worship a week competes with hours a day of designed practice, and the room needs to feel that mismatch. Point out that many of these practices were built by people who understand desire and profit from it. The shaping isn't accidental.

discussion.q: Plenty of sensible people say a phone is just a neutral tool. What's true in that? Where does the tool stop being neutral and start aiming you?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. A device can be used well, and panic that treats it as pure evil is neither true nor useful. Then press on what makes this tool different: it's built to hold attention, it learns what holds yours, and it gives you more of it. Help the room tell the difference between using a tool and being used by one.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 115:4-8. Setting aside the word "worship" for a moment, what are you giving yourself to every day, and what is it slowly making you into?
discussion.behind: This is the center. Some will resist calling a phone worship, so let them see the mechanism first: sustained attention and trust work like worship whatever we call them, and the psalm's law holds. Ask what character the daily habit is producing, whether distraction, envy, outrage or restlessness, and let the answer sit.

discussion.q: The deeper cost may be less the time we lose than the wants we pick up: distraction over presence, the edited life over the given one. Which of those trained wants do you recognize in yourself?
discussion.behind: Go first. Name a want the screen has trained in you. Then invite the room past the familiar guilt about screen time into the harder question of what they now want, and when they started wanting it.

objections.objection: Technology is neutral. A phone is a tool like a hammer or a car, and blaming the device is a cop-out for people who lack self-control. The problem is the person, not the thing.
objections.response: There's a real point here. A device can be used well, personal responsibility is real, and a study that blamed a rectangle for every human failure would be letting people off the hook. But the neutral-tool argument breaks on what's different about this tool. A hammer doesn't buzz in your pocket all day. It doesn't run on systems built by people who study what captures attention and serve you more of it to keep you scrolling. Many of these products are designed to capture and hold attention because attention is what they sell. That isn't neutral. It's aimed. Responsibility isn't the opposite of seeing that. Responsibility starts with seeing clearly what you're up against, so you stop bringing a lecture about willpower to a contest the tool was built to win.

objections.objection: This is just nostalgia and fear of change. Every generation panics about new technology. They said the same about novels and television, and it turned out fine. This is moral panic dressed up as theology.
objections.response: The caution is fair, and the history is real. Every era has had its prophets of doom about a new medium, many were wrong, and a Christianity that's merely afraid of the present has confused the gospel with nostalgia. But noticing a pattern of past panics doesn't show that this concern is one of them. The better response is to look at the evidence. Researchers with no theological stake have argued that attention, anxiety and friendship among the young have shifted alongside the smartphone and the feed. Some of those findings are debated, and they should be held carefully. The task is neither panic nor denial. It's the harder middle thing: take the strongest secular account of what these tools do, hold it up to what Scripture says about the heart, and respond with practice rather than with fear or a shrug.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If someone could see only your search history and your screen time for the last month, with no explanation, what would they conclude you love, and would they be wrong?
sessions.practice: This week, name one habit you never chose, like the morning scroll, the reach at every red light, or the feed you open without deciding to. Once a day, at the exact moment you'd usually reach for the screen, do something else instead: a minute of prayer, a minute of silence, or a real look at a real person. Don't try to quit anything. Just put one chosen practice where the automatic one usually lives, and write down what you feel when you refuse the reflex.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we never sat down and chose to be shaped by these things, and that's what frightens us, that we're being made into someone by a thousand habits we never looked at. We reach for the glowing screen before we reach for you, and we've grown restless and distracted and hungry for a life that's always somewhere else. Forgive us for giving our attention to altars we'd never name out loud. Show us what these habits are making us into, and give us the courage to interrupt them, not in panic and not in pride, but as people who want to be aimed at you again. You made us to become like what we worship. Turn our worship home. Amen.
reflection: What habit am I running every day that I never chose, and what has it been training me to want?
If we become like what we give ourselves to, what am I becoming, and would I want the people who watch me to become the same thing by the same means?
Where have I told myself the device is neutral so I wouldn't have to look at what it's doing to my heart?
sessions.teaching:
Many of us reach for the phone the moment we wake, before we pray, before we speak to anyone we love, before our feet find the floor, and we never decided to. That's worth sitting with. I'd call it a liturgy, and I mean the word carefully. In the old sense a liturgy is a repeated, bodily, shared practice that trains the people who do it to love something, to want a particular picture of the good life so deeply that they no longer have to think about wanting it. The church has always known that practices shape loves. That's why it gave people not only doctrines to believe but a Table to come to, water to be washed in, and prayers to say until they became the shape of a heart.

What James K.A. Smith noticed, and what ought to unsettle us, is that much of the shaping in our lives isn't happening in church. It's happening at the mall and on the screen, in practices every bit as liturgical as anything in a sanctuary and far more frequent. In Desiring the Kingdom he walks a reader through a shopping mall as if it were a cathedral: images of the good life on every wall, the message that you're incomplete and this will complete you, the ritual of buying. Then he asks what such a place is training us to love. The screen does the same work, except it never closes. It doesn't stay behind at the store. It comes home in your pocket and lies on the pillow beside you. So the question isn't whether you're being formed. You are, every day. The question is by what, and toward what.

Scripture has a blunt line about this. Psalm 115 describes the idols of the nations, with mouths that don't speak and eyes that don't see, and then says, "Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them" (Psalm 115:8). That's a law of formation stated plainly. We take on the character of whatever we give ourselves to. Serve an idol that can't see or hear, and you grow blind and deaf to God like the thing you serve. Give yourself every day to something built to scatter attention and stir up wanting, and you'll slowly become scattered and wanting. It doesn't have to call itself worship to work like worship.

Here's the strongest case on the other side, because many sensible people make it. A phone is a tool, they say, as neutral as a hammer, and the only question is whether you use it well. Blaming the device is an excuse for people who lack discipline. Some of that is true. A device can be used well, and responsibility is real. A study that blamed a rectangle for the whole of the human heart would be lying.

But the argument breaks on one fact. This tool isn't much like a hammer. A hammer doesn't buzz in your pocket all day. It wasn't designed by teams of gifted people who study how attention works and who earn more the longer they can hold yours. The screen learns you. It watches what stops your thumb and gives you more of it, and it's very good at that, because that's what it's for. Neutral is the last thing it is.

I have to be careful here, because I'm not describing other people. I'm describing the pastor who tells his church to seek first the kingdom and then lies in the dark scrolling until his eyes burn. I'm describing parents who feel their patience and their stillness wear thin year by year, and who watch their children learn that the right response to a moment of boredom is to reach for the thing in your pocket. Most of us know the feeling.

So here's the weight of this session. The problem isn't mainly the time. Everyone talks about the hours lost, and that's real, but it's the shallow version of the loss. The deeper problem is the loves we pick up. These habits are training our hearts, patiently and well, to prefer distraction to presence, outrage to patience, comparison to gratitude, and the edited life on the screen to the actual life in front of us, which will never look as bright. We didn't choose to want those things. We were trained to, one unchosen repetition at a time, and the training worked. Paul assumed as much when he wrote, "Do not be conformed to this world" (Romans 12:2). Left alone, we'll be conformed.

That isn't a call to throw the phone in a lake, which usually lasts a weekend and changes nothing. It's a call to wake up to a shaping that's been happening in the dark, to name the habits we never chose, and to begin the older work of choosing what we'll be formed by.

scriptureStudy.note: "Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them." We're conformed to the character of whatever we serve. A habit built on distraction produces distracted people, and one built on comparison produces envious ones.

"You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image." The first commands are about where worship is aimed, and they assume people will always worship something. The only question is what.

"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind." Paul names two pressures, the shaping of the age and the transforming work of God, and assumes that if we do nothing, we'll be conformed.

"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth." Setting the mind is a repeated act of attention. It assumes attention drifts downward on its own and has to be aimed upward again and again.
"No one can serve two masters ... You cannot serve God and money." The heart can't be split, so the daily habits of buying and comparing aren't harmless side interests. They're rival masters.

John names "the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life." These are old appetites, and much of what fills our screens is built to feed exactly these three: wanting, looking and comparing.

"Their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things." Paul describes formation gone wrong: appetites that have become a god because minds have been trained downward.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take the secular observers at their strongest, because people outside the church have seen a great deal here. The task is to hold their findings up to Scripture rather than either baptizing them or brushing them off. Smith supplies the frame in Desiring the Kingdom and You Are What You Love: cultural liturgies, practices like the mall, the stadium and the feed that work as rituals aiming our love at a rival picture of flourishing. His reading of the shopping mall is worth walking through slowly.

Set beside it Neil Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death (1985), which argued that a medium shapes a culture as much as its content does, and that a people formed by entertainment will expect everything, truth and worship included, to entertain them. Then bring in the more recent argument, made by Jonathan Haidt among others, that rising anxiety and changing friendships among adolescents track the arrival of the smartphone and the algorithmic feed. Some researchers dispute how strong that link is, and a group should know that. Even where it holds, it names a symptom; it can't supply a cure for a disordered love.

Blaise Pascal saw the root long before any of this. In the Pensées he wrote about diversion, our dread of sitting quietly alone in a room and the busy activity we invent to avoid it. The screen is only the newest and most efficient answer to an old human fear. The aim isn't to arrive at a rule about screen time. It's to see the mechanism and ask the question underneath: what picture of the good life is this habit selling me, and would I choose it if it showed me its price?
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a younger woman in your group grows defensive when the session turns to phones. Her whole social world lives on her devices, she says: her friendships, her family far away, her sense of belonging. The older people in the room don't understand that for her generation there's no clean line between online and real life, and all this worry feels like judgment from people who don't need what she needs.

Hear her first, and say she's right about what's real. The connection is real and the friendships are real. A dismissive lecture from someone who grew up without any of this will land as exactly the judgment she fears, and it'll teach her the church has nothing useful to say.

But the session isn't asking her to prove the tool is all bad. It's asking a question that applies to her precisely because she's on it most: what is this practice training her to love? Has constant connection also trained a constant anxiety? Has the belonging it offers also taught her that she's only as loved as her last post did well? Don't let the generational point close the question. Honor her need for connection, then ask gently whether the thing meeting that need is also forming a hunger it can never satisfy. Ask the rest of the room the same question about their own habits.

sessions.title: Counter-Formation: Why the Church Has Always Had Disciplines
sessions.aim: To recover the historic spiritual disciplines, not as a hobby for spiritual athletes but as ordinary Christian counter-formation: chosen practices that re-aim a heart the world has been aiming all week. The session refuses both the legalism that turns them into a performance and the passivity that waits to be changed while practicing nothing.
sessions.summary:
If we're shaped all day by habits we didn't choose, the obvious question is what the church has always done about it. The answer is the spiritual disciplines, and the word makes many of us flinch. Some hear monks in caves. Others hear the grim, joyless legalism they left behind.

That suspicion deserves a hearing, because the disciplines have been abused, turned into a ladder for feeling superior or a currency for buying what was already free. But that was never what they were for. Dallas Willard recovered their real logic for our time: we can't expect to act like Jesus in the hard moment if we haven't arranged our lives like his in the ordinary ones. He drew a line between trying and training. You can't try your way into patience under pressure any more than you can try your way through a marathon you never trained for.

Richard Foster mapped the practices the church has kept, from prayer and fasting and study to solitude, service, confession and worship. They work as counter-liturgies. And they're neither a performance for God's approval nor magic. They're training, the arranging of a life so grace already given can reach the places willpower never touches. We don't practice to become someone God will finally love. We practice because there's no other way a love gets into the muscles.

keyScripture.why: "But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified" (1 Corinthians 9:27). Paul takes the athlete's training as his own model: a deliberate discipline of the body and its habits, not a hope that character will simply arrive.

discussion.q: What's your gut reaction to the phrase "spiritual disciplines"? Where did that reaction come from?
discussion.behind: Start by letting the baggage out, because most people carry some. Some hear duty without joy, some hear spiritual elitism, some hear a legalism they fled. Naming the reaction clears the ground, so the room can hear what the disciplines actually are instead of fighting a caricature.

discussion.q: Willard distinguished trying from training: no one tries their way through a marathon they never trained for. Where in your life have you tried again and again to be different, in a place where you've never actually trained?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Most people have one recurring failure they attack with fresh resolve every few months and never with a change of practice. Help the room see that trying without training is the frustration they already know, and that the disciplines are the training they've skipped.

discussion.q: The disciplines have been turned into a ladder for feeling superior or a way to earn grace. Where have you seen that, or felt it in yourself? What did it do to the practice?
discussion.behind: Take the critique seriously. The disciplines really have been used for pride and for earning, and pretending otherwise would make people defensive. Let the damage be named fully, so that when you recover the true purpose it doesn't sound like a denial of what the counterfeit has done.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 9:24-27. Foster names practices like solitude, silence, fasting and study. Which one unsettles you most, and what might that discomfort say about what you've been formed to need?
discussion.behind: The discipline a person most resists is often aimed at his deepest disorder. Fear of silence, fasting or being alone often shows what we've been using to fill or numb ourselves. Help people read their resistance as information. Don't push anyone into a practice they aren't ready for.

discussion.q: How does it change your willingness to try a discipline if it's training and not a test you can fail?
discussion.behind: Many people avoid the disciplines because they hear them as one more way to be judged. Seen as training undertaken by someone already loved, they lose their threat. Go first. Name a discipline you practice badly and unevenly, and show that the point is training, not performance.

objections.objection: This is works-righteousness with a nicer name. We're saved by grace, not by fasting and praying and keeping a list. Adding all these practices turns the free gift back into a religion of earning.
objections.response: This objection protects the center of the gospel, and it must never be given up. We're saved by grace through faith and not by any practice, and the moment a discipline becomes the price of God's acceptance it has become an idol and a lie. But it assumes a choice between grace and practice that the New Testament doesn't make. The same Paul who staked everything on grace wrote, "I discipline my body and keep it under control" (1 Corinthians 9:27), and told Timothy, "train yourself for godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7). The disciplines aren't how we earn the love. They're how a love already given gets down into a self that grace has claimed but not yet fully remade. Think of the difference between earning a gift and learning to use it. A person given a piano doesn't earn it by practicing, but without practice the gift stays silent. The disciplines are practice, not payment.

objections.objection: I've tried spiritual disciplines and I always fail. I start a plan, keep it for a week, life happens, and I quit and feel worse than before. They just don't work for an ordinary busy person.
objections.response: That discouragement is real and common, and it's usually the fruit of bad instruction, not of some flaw in you. Most people fail for two fixable reasons. The first is size: they attempt a program built for a monk, an hour of silence and a day of fasting, collapse under it in a week, and decide they can't do any of it, when a small practice would have held. That's next week's whole subject. The second is that they treat the disciplines as a test to pass rather than training to build, so a missed day feels like a judgment on them instead of what it is, a Tuesday. An athlete who misses a workout doesn't decide he isn't an athlete. He trains again the next day. Coming back, over and over, is itself the training.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the one place in your life you keep trying to change by sheer resolve, and what practice have you never once been willing to build there?
sessions.practice: This week, choose one discipline in its smallest form and practice it daily, badly if need be, without measuring how well it goes. Five minutes of silence with no phone in the room. One meal given to prayer instead of food. Ten minutes in a Gospel with nothing to produce from it. Don't aim to feel anything. Aim only to keep the appointment, and write down what you notice in yourself when you arrange your day around God instead of waiting to feel moved.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we've been trying to be different for years, and trying isn't working, because you never meant us to try our way into a life we've never trained for. Forgive us for looking down on the practices your church has always kept, whether because someone made them into a ladder or because we were afraid of what silence and fasting would show us about ourselves. Teach us that these practices aren't the price of your love but the way your love reaches the parts of us willpower never touches. Give us the courage to be beginners, to practice badly, to start before we feel like it. Train us, patiently, into the people you've already called us to be. Amen.
reflection: Where have I mistaken repeated trying for training, attacking the same failure with fresh resolve and never with a changed practice?
Which discipline do I most resist, and what might that resistance show about what I've been using to fill or numb myself?
Have I avoided the disciplines because I heard them as a test I could fail? What would change if I heard them as training I'm only beginning?
sessions.teaching:
Once we've seen the habits shaping us all day without our consent, we come to the obvious question: what do we do about it? The answer the church has given for two thousand years is a word that makes a lot of modern Christians flinch. The word is discipline. Say "spiritual disciplines" in most rooms and you can watch people brace. Some hear monks in caves, a kind of athletic spirituality for specialists that has nothing to do with someone running carpool and answering email. Others hear something worse: a grim religion of duty and measurement, of looking over your shoulder to see who's holier, the very thing some of them left church to escape.

That second suspicion isn't paranoid. The disciplines really have been abused. They've been made into a ladder people climb to feel superior to those on the lower rungs, and into a currency for buying a favor that was never for sale. Jesus warned about exactly this when he told his disciples not to pray and fast "that they may be seen by others" (Matthew 6:5; compare 6:16). A fast that makes you proud has done you more harm than the skipped meal ever could, and a prayer life kept as a scoreboard is closer to the sin it means to fight than to God. All of that is real. None of it is what the disciplines are.

Dallas Willard's gift to our generation was to recover their actual logic for people who had only seen the counterfeit. His question is simple enough to disarm you. Why do we expect to act like Jesus in the hard moment when we've made no effort to live like him in all the easy ones? We want to answer an insult with grace, a crisis with peace, a temptation with freedom, right on the spot, and we can't, and we conclude we've failed. The truth is that we never trained.

That's where Willard drew the line this session turns on, between trying and training. No one tries their way through a marathon. You don't stand at the start of twenty-six miles, having never run, and simply resolve very sincerely to want it badly enough. You'd collapse in the first mile, and your sincerity wouldn't save you. What carries a runner is months of ordinary practice on ordinary days, which built a body that can do in the race what effort alone never could. Paul used the same picture. "Every athlete exercises self-control in all things," he wrote, and then, about himself, "I discipline my body and keep it under control" (1 Corinthians 9:25, 27). Jesus assumed it too: "everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher" (Luke 6:40). Somehow we've believed the Christian life is the one place where training doesn't apply.

Richard Foster, in Celebration of Discipline (1978), mapped the practices the church has used for this training. He grouped them as inward (meditation, prayer, fasting, study), outward (simplicity, solitude, submission, service) and corporate (confession, worship, guidance, celebration). Willard sorted them another way, into disciplines of abstinence, where we deliberately go without, like solitude, silence and fasting, and disciplines of engagement, where we deliberately take something up, like study, worship and service. The two work together, emptying and filling, the way breathing does.

It helps to hear them as counter-liturgies, each set against something the world is training into us. The world has spent all week teaching you to reach for your phone in every silence; solitude teaches you to sit in the silence and find God there. The culture says every appetite must be fed the moment it speaks; fasting teaches you that you aren't your appetites' servant. Against a feed that manufactures envy, worship trains gratitude. Against a life of constant diversion, meditation on Scripture trains attention. Even Jesus kept these rhythms: "rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed" (Mark 1:35).

Now the caution this session has been building toward, and I include myself in it, because none of us practices this well enough to sound like an expert. The disciplines aren't a performance that makes God love you. If you take one thing from tonight, take that. God isn't more pleased with the version of you that fasted this week and less pleased with the one that didn't. His pleasure in you was settled at the cross. And the disciplines aren't magic either, levers you pull to force a result, because the change is always God's gift.

So what are they? They're training: the deliberate arranging of a life so that grace already given can reach the places willpower has never touched, the reflexes and appetites and buried loves that no amount of trying has moved. Hebrews is plain that it's hard: "For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it" (Hebrews 12:11). We don't train in order to become someone God will finally accept. We train because we've already been accepted, and there's no other way a love that real gets into the muscles of an ordinary life.

scriptureStudy.note: "Every athlete exercises self-control in all things." Paul reaches for the trained competitor, whose freedom in the contest was won by discipline long before, as a picture of the Christian life.
"I discipline my body and keep it under control." The apostle of grace doesn't think training is beneath him or against grace. He treats it as the ordinary shape of following Jesus.
"Everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher." Jesus assumes discipleship is an apprenticeship, and its outcome is likeness to the teacher, which never comes by admiration alone.
"Solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice." Maturity is the fruit of constant practice, a trained discernment built over time.
"For while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way." Paul grants the worth of physical training and says the same logic applies, with higher stakes, to godliness.

"And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed." Jesus himself kept solitude and prayer, arranging his days around time with the Father.

"For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it." Discipline is named as hard now and fruitful later, and the fruit belongs to the trained.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, read the two writers who recovered this teaching for the modern church, and read them against the longer tradition behind them. In The Spirit of the Disciplines (1988), Dallas Willard argued that spiritual change follows the same logic as any other formation: we're shaped by what we practice, and the disciplines are best understood not as heroic feats but as ordinary training by which a life is arranged to receive grace. His two lists are a useful map. The disciplines of abstinence are solitude, silence, fasting, frugality, chastity, secrecy and sacrifice; the disciplines of engagement are study, worship, celebration, service, prayer, fellowship, confession and submission. Ask which list your group has neglected. Most of us are far more at ease taking things up than going without, and it's the going without that most directly pushes back on how we've been formed.

Richard Foster's Celebration of Discipline (1978) brought these practices back to a wide Protestant readership that had largely lost them, and its title makes the point that discipline and celebration aren't opposites. Set both books against what they draw on: the desert fathers and mothers of the third and fourth centuries, who went into the wilderness to be remade, and Benedict of Nursia, whose sixth-century Rule ordered a whole life around prayer, work and reading. Keep the gospel guardrail in front the whole way. The disciplines answer grace and never buy it, and Willard himself insisted that grace is opposed to earning, not to effort, which is the door into the next session.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group is drawn to the disciplines in a way that worries you a little. She lights up, takes notes, and by the end has sketched an ambitious plan: an hour of prayer each morning, a weekly fast, an hour of study every day. She's clearly someone who does things thoroughly and well.

Her eagerness is a real grace, and you don't want to dampen it. But you can see two dangers. The first is plain overreach, a program so large it will likely fall apart within two weeks and leave her sure she's failed. That's next session's concern, and it's worth mentioning now. The second is subtler: a capable, high-achieving person can turn the disciplines into one more place to perform, measure and quietly rank herself, which is exactly the abuse this session warned about.

Honor her hunger, because a heart that wants to order its life around God is a beautiful thing. Then ask her two questions. Is the plan small enough to survive a hard week? And can she tell the difference between practicing because she's loved and practicing to feel she's earned it? The same disciplines that free a humble heart can bind an ambitious one, and the difference isn't in the practice but in what it rests on. Ask the group which of those two dangers they recognize in themselves.
